body: AI Development That Starts With the User, Not Just the Model.

Artificial intelligence is transforming how products work. But most AI-first products fail because they prioritize the model over the human. We do the opposite: we design AI-powered products that users actually want to use. From AI product strategy and UX design to rapid prototyping and production-ready applications, we combine design-led thinking with development expertise to help startups and innovation teams build AI products that work.

sections.heading: Why Design-Led AI Development Produces Better Products
body: AI development without design thinking leads to overly complex interfaces, poor user experiences, and products that fail to gain adoption. When design leads, you get:
•	Clearer workflows around AI features — users understand what the AI can do and how to use it.
•	Better onboarding and activation — people get value from the AI immediately, not after months of frustration.
•	Smarter feature prioritization — focus on AI capabilities users actually need, not just technically impressive ones.
•	Faster time to market — a clear product vision accelerates both design and development.
•	Stronger product differentiation — thoughtful UX around AI features creates defensible competitive advantage.

sections.heading: Our AI Development Services
body: AI Product Strategy

We help you define what your AI product is actually solving. We map out the user journey, identify where AI creates value, and make clear decisions about what to build first. This prevents scope creep and keeps development focused.
UX for AI-Powered Interfaces

Designing interfaces for AI systems is different from traditional UX. Users need to understand AI outputs, know how to refine them, and trust the system. We design interfaces that make AI logic transparent, support human-in-the-loop workflows, and minimize confusion.
AI Feature Design

Whether you're adding an AI assistant, building recommendation engines, or integrating LLMs into your product, we design the UX around those features. We consider input formatting, output presentation, fallback states, and user education.
Rapid Prototyping & MVP Development

Get from idea to a working prototype quickly. We design interactive prototypes that demonstrate AI-powered workflows, test assumptions with users, and inform development roadmaps. For startups that need production-ready MVPs, we pair design with development to build and launch.
AI Feature Testing & Refinement

Once your AI product launches, we help you refine it based on user behavior. We identify where users struggle with AI outputs, where trust breaks down, and where you need better explanations or controls.

body: Hero / Introduction

Design is not magic. It's a discipline: research, strategy, iteration, measurement, and continuous improvement. But many organisations treat design as decoration—a last-minute polish instead of a strategic practice. If that's where you are, your products are suffering. Your team isn't confident. Your delivery is slow.

Design maturity is the journey from design-as-decoration to design-as-strategy. It's about building the team, processes, and culture to make better product decisions faster. We help organisations move up that curve.
What Design Capability Building Looks Like
Design maturity isn't a destination; it's an evolution. We help you move through stages:
Level 1 (Ad-hoc): Design is project-based or freelance. No shared process. No research. No measurement.
Level 2 (Emerging): A small design team exists. Some process. Basic research and testing. Inconsistent measurement.
Level 3 (Established): Design is embedded in product teams. Clear process. Regular research and testing. Metrics inform decisions.
Level 4 (Strategic): Design leads business outcomes. Research is continuous. Design decisions are strategic. Teams are confident and empowered.
Level 5 (Optimised): Design is ingrained in culture. Continuous experimentation and measurement. Cross-functional alignment and ownership.
Our Services
Maturity Assessment
We audit your design practice: team structure, processes, tools, research, measurement, and culture. We deliver a detailed assessment and a prioritised roadmap for improvement.
Team Coaching and Mentorship
We work alongside your design team to build skills, confidence, and leadership. Monthly coaching sessions, design critiques, and mentorship.
Process Design and Documentation
We help you design your design process: discovery, user research, design phases, feedback loops, launch, and measurement. Customised to your organisation.
Design Operations (DesignOps)
We set up tools, workflows, and governance: design systems, design tokens, file management, design review processes, hiring and onboarding.
Hiring and Interview Support
We help you define design roles, write job descriptions, review portfolios, and conduct interviews to build the right team.
Workshops and Capability Building
We run workshops on research, user testing, design thinking, accessibility, design systems, and leadership. Customised to your team's needs.
Who This Is For

You're a design director, chief product officer, or digital transformation lead who recognises that your design practice is holding you back. You want to invest in building a stronger, more mature design capability. You're not looking for quick fixes; you're looking for sustainable change.
Common Maturity Challenges
Design team lacks confidence
Designers don't have a seat at the table. Product and engineering call the shots. We help build confidence and create a culture where design drives decisions.
No shared design process
Every project is different. Some teams do research; others don't. There's no consistency. We define a scalable, repeatable process.
Design and engineering are misaligned
Designers and engineers speak different languages. Design decisions are questioned or reworked. We create shared processes and language.
Design research is ad-hoc or missing
Teams skip research because they're in a hurry. We help you build research into your rhythm—continuous user testing, regular interviews, metrics.
Onboarding and scaling is difficult
New designers struggle to understand your practices and tools. We help you build documentation, mentorship, and clear DesignOps.
No measurement or ROI for design
It's unclear if design is actually delivering business value. We help you define metrics and measure impact.

design-system-consulting.metaDescription: Design system consulting for product teams scaling their design and development. We build, audit, and improve design systems that reduce inconsistency and accelerate delivery.

body: Hero / Introduction

Your product is growing. Your design team is growing. Your codebase is growing. And inconsistency is growing with it. Components that look slightly different. Design decisions that aren't documented. Engineers guessing at spacing and colour. A design system solves this: it's the single source of truth for design and development, shared across teams.
We help product teams build, audit, and improve design systems that reduce rework, accelerate delivery, and create shared language across design and engineering.
What a Design System Is and Why It Matters at Scale
A design system is a collection of reusable components, patterns, tokens, and guidelines—shared by design and engineering to build consistent, scalable products.
The benefits:
•	Consistency: Users see a coherent experience across products and platforms
•	Speed: Designers and engineers reuse tested components instead of rebuilding from scratch
•	Reduced rework: Decisions are documented and shared—no more "which button style did we use?"
•	Confidence: Teams trust the system and can ship faster
•	Scaling: As your product and team grow, the system grows with you
Our Design System Services
Build from Scratch
If you don't have a design system, we create one. We audit your existing product, extract patterns, define tokens, build a component library, and document everything.
Audit and Assessment
We assess your existing design system: Is it being used? Is it documented? Are tokens and components consistent? What's broken? We deliver a priority-ranked improvement roadmap.
Document and Extend
We take your existing components and patterns, formalise them, document them (in Figma, Storybook, or both), and build out missing pieces.
Design Tokens and Component Architecture
We define design tokens (colours, typography, spacing, shadows) and build component hierarchies that scale. Tokens flow from design to code automatically.
Handoff and Team Training
We train your team on how to use, maintain, and evolve the system. We don't leave you with a document; we leave you with ownership.
Who Needs a Design System
If any of the following applies, you need a design system:
•	You have more than one designer
•	You have more than one engineer working on UI
•	You're shipping features faster than documentation can keep up
•	You're working across multiple platforms (web, iOS, Android)
•	You want consistency but don't have a shared language between design and engineering
Design systems scale with team and product growth. The best time to start is when you first feel inconsistency. The next best time is now.
Common Design System Problems We Solve
Scattered design decisions
Components are built differently in different parts of the codebase. There's no single source of truth. We centralise and document.
Duplicated work
Designers keep redesigning buttons and forms. Engineers keep rebuilding components. We create reusable, tested components.
Inconsistent user experience
Different parts of your product feel like different products. We define and enforce consistency across the system.
Slow feature development
Teams spend time debating design decisions that should already be solved. We document decisions so teams move fast.
Design and engineering misalignment
Designers create one thing; engineers build something different. We create a shared system and language.
What You Get
•	A comprehensive design audit and inventory of existing components
•	A defined set of design tokens (colours, typography, spacing, etc.)
•	A component library in Figma, React Storybook, or both
•	Documentation and usage guidelines for each component
•	A token distribution system (Figma → CSS/code automation)
•	A roadmap for system evolution and maintenance
•	Team training and knowledge transfer
Call to Action

body: UX Research Agency. Reduce Risk, Validate Decisions, Build With Confidence.
What UX Research Delivers for Your Business
Designing without research is guessing. UX research gives you evidence.

It answers the questions that keep product leaders awake: Are users actually struggling with this? Will they pay for this feature? Why are they abandoning our checkout? What do our competitors do better?

Whether you're early-stage and need to validate a core assumption, or enterprise and scaling across markets, research grounds your decisions, reduces wasted development, and improves the odds of success.

sections.heading: Our Research Services
body: User Interviews & Contextual Inquiry

We talk to your users in depth—either in person, over video, or in their natural environment. We understand their goals, frustrations, workflows, and mental models. This feeds strategy, informs design, and surfaces opportunities.
Usability Testing

We recruit users, run moderated sessions (or unmoderated remote tests), and measure whether they can complete tasks, where they struggle, and what confuses them. Fast feedback on your designs before you launch.
Survey Design & Analysis
We design quantitative research to validate patterns from interviews, measure satisfaction, or understand market segments. We handle recruitment, analysis, and reporting.
Heuristic & Accessibility Reviews
We audit your product against UX best practices and accessibility standards (WCAG). This catches low-hanging fruit before testing.
Competitive Benchmarking
We analyse how competitors solve similar problems, measure their features, and identify opportunities for differentiation.
Research Synthesis & Reporting
We turn raw data into insights: journey maps, persona updates, opportunity statements, and clear recommendations for the design or product team.
When to Commission UX Research
Research is most valuable at these moments:
•	Before a redesign, to understand current user pain points and priorities
•	Early in product development, to validate assumptions before you code
•	Before a major feature launch, to test with real users first
•	After launch, to measure adoption and identify support friction
•	When you're entering a new market or audience segment
•	When stakeholders disagree and data can settle the debate
The best time to do research is when someone is about to make a high-stakes decision with incomplete information.
Who We Work With
We run research for:
•	Product teams at startups validating product-market fit
•	Mid-market companies scaling features and entering new markets
•	Enterprise organisations rolling out UX improvements across teams
•	In-house teams upskilling and running their own research
•	Agencies and consultants who outsource research to us

sections.heading: Our Approach to Research
body: Methodologically Sound
We use proven methods (interviews, moderated testing, surveys) tailored to your question. We report confidence levels and limitations. No fluff, no bias.
Efficient & Budget-Conscious
We design research that answers your specific questions without unnecessary scope creep. 5 users in a usability test often reveals 80% of issues. We optimise sample size and methodology for budget.
Fast Turnaround

Actionable Insights
We don't just say "users are confused." We tell you where they're confused, why, and what specific design change will fix it.
Mix of Qualitative & Quantitative
We combine interviews and observation (why people do things) with surveys and metrics (how many do it). The combination is more powerful than either alone.

faqs.question: What UX research methods do you use?

faqs.question: What's the difference between UX research and usability testing?
faqs.answer: Usability testing is one type of UX research. It measures whether users can use your product. UX research is broader: it explores user needs, motivations, workflows, and pain points. We often combine both.

faqs.question: Can you help us set up an ongoing research practice?
faqs.answer: Yes. We can train your team, help you build a research process, and hand off recruitment and testing. We can also embed with your team and run research continuously on a retainer basis.

faqs.question: How many research participants do I need?
faqs.answer: It depends on your question. Usability testing: 5–8 users catches most issues. User interviews: 10–15 uncovers patterns. Surveys: 50–200+ for quantitative validation. We help you right-size based on your goals and budget.

body: B2B E-Commerce UX Design | Sand Dollar Design
B2B e-commerce UX design for distributors, manufacturers, and wholesale platforms. We design complex ordering interfaces that reduce friction and increase order volume.
B2B E-Commerce UX Design

B2B e-commerce is fundamentally different from B2C. Your customers are buying in bulk, managing multiple locations, working with approval workflows, and integrating with their own systems. Generic e-commerce UX fails in this context.

We design B2B platforms that serve distributors, manufacturers, and wholesale companies. We understand order complexity, account management, pricing tiers, and the business workflows your customers actually follow. We've redesigned FMCG distribution platforms that increased order volume and reduced buying friction.
How B2B E-Commerce UX Differs from B2C
Account structure is complex

B2C has one user, one account. B2B has multiple users per company, different roles, approval hierarchies, and cost centre allocation. Your UX needs to serve procurement teams, approvers, and finance teams with different needs.
Bulk ordering with custom pricing

B2C shoppers buy retail quantities at listed prices. B2B customers order in cases, pallets, or containers. Pricing varies by customer, order size, and contract terms. Your interface needs to handle complex pricing without confusing users.
Approval workflows are essential
Large orders often require approval before purchase. Your platform needs to route orders for approval, show approval status, and handle rejections gracefully.
Integration with backend systems
Your B2B customers use ERPs, accounting systems, and inventory management tools. Your platform needs to integrate with these systems or at least make data export easy.
Sales team involvement varies
Some B2B customers are fully self-service. Others rely on their account manager. Your UX needs to serve both—with sales team tools and self-service ordering.
Buyers know what they want
B2B buyers are usually professionals familiar with your products. They don't need extensive product education; they need fast ordering and transparency. Your UX should respect their expertise.
Our B2B E-Commerce UX Services
Platform design and redesign
We design B2B e-commerce platforms from scratch or redesign existing ones. We map ordering workflows, account structures, and approval processes. We design interfaces that serve multiple user types.
Ordering interface simplification

Complex ordering interfaces cause friction and lost orders. We redesign ordering flows so professional buyers can place orders quickly. Bulk uploads, quick reorders, saved carts—all optimised for speed.
Account and user management
Multi-user B2B accounts are complex. We design account management dashboards that let administrators manage users, permissions, approval rules, and account settings.
Pricing and promotion management
B2B pricing varies by customer, volume, and contract. We design interfaces that display the right prices for each customer without confusing them. Promotions and discounts are clear.
Integration design
Your platform needs to exchange data with customer ERPs and systems. We design integration interfaces, data mapping tools, and API documentation that makes connections smooth.
Marketplace platform strategy
If you're building a multi-supplier B2B marketplace, we design the buyer experience, supplier experience, and admin tools that manage the network.
B2B E-Commerce Challenges We Solve
Complex ordering workflows
Bulk ordering with approvals, custom pricing, and integration requirements is complex. We simplify these workflows so buyers can order efficiently.
Account and permission management
Managing multiple users with different permissions across multiple locations is tedious. We design admin tools that make account management fast.
Pricing transparency
Customers don't understand their pricing. Volume discounts, promotional pricing, and contract terms are opaque. We design pricing interfaces that are transparent and customer-specific.
ERP integration friction
Connecting your platform to customer ERP systems is complex. We design integration workflows and data mapping tools that reduce friction.
Sales team vs. self-service balance
Some customers want to order online; others want sales team support. We design platforms that serve both, with sales tools and self-service ordering coexisting.
Who This Is For
Food and beverage distributors
FMCG distribution is a classic B2B e-commerce use case. We've designed ordering platforms for distributors that increased online order volume and reduced manual order entry.
Manufacturing platforms
Manufacturers selling components or finished goods to business customers need platforms that handle complex product configurations, bulk ordering, and approval workflows.
Wholesale and distribution networks
Wholesalers moving to online need B2B platforms that serve their channel partners. We design these platforms to increase partner adoption and order velocity.
Marketplace platforms
If you're building a multi-supplier marketplace, we design the buyer, supplier, and admin experiences. Think Alibaba or Faire, but for your industry.
Case Study: Heineken
We redesigned a major FMCG B2B e-commerce platform for a global beverage company. The platform serves distributors and retailers ordering in bulk.
Challenge: The existing platform was complex and outdated. Buyers struggled with ordering, pricing was unclear, and bulk uploads didn't work well.

Solution: We simplified the ordering interface, redesigned bulk upload workflows, and made pricing transparent. We designed account management tools so distributors could manage multi-location ordering.
Outcome: Online order volume increased 35% within 6 months. Order placement time dropped by 40%. Support ticket volume decreased as users found answers in the new interface.

We start by understanding your business model. We interview your sales team, your biggest customers, and your operations team. We learn how orders flow through your system today.
We map current ordering workflows and identify friction. We research competitor platforms. We prototype solutions and test with real customers.
We design platforms that serve multiple user types: buyers, approvers, account managers, and admins. We create systems documentation so your team can evolve the platform.

body: Banking UX Consulting | Sand Dollar Design
Banking UX consulting for retail and corporate banks. We improve digital banking journeys, redesign legacy interfaces, and support CX transformation programmes.
Banking UX Consulting

Banking has never moved faster. Your customers expect seamless digital experiences on par with tech companies. Meanwhile, your legacy systems, regulatory constraints, and risk-averse culture make change difficult.

We help retail and corporate banks close the gap between customer expectations and operational reality. We've helped banks redesign onboarding flows, modernise mobile apps, and rethink digital banking strategy. We understand retail banking, corporate banking, private banking, and the emerging neobank challenge.
The Banking UX Challenge
Digital banking is no longer a competitive advantage—it's table stakes. But executing it at scale, across legacy infrastructure and regulatory complexity, is harder than it looks.
Customers expect frictionless journeys

Your new banking customers have used Revolut, Wise, and other neobanks. They expect instant account opening, mobile-first interfaces, and real-time notifications. Traditional banks with slower onboarding and dated interfaces lose customers to digital-first competitors.
Legacy platforms constrain innovation

Your core banking system was built in the 1990s. It's stable, it works, but it doesn't talk to modern front-ends. A new customer app has to work *around* these systems, introducing complexity and friction. Good banking UX design navigates these constraints without exposing them to users.
Trust and security cannot be afterthoughts

Unlike fintechs, banks carry regulatory weight. Your users expect security as a given, but they also don't want to feel like they're jumping through hoops. Multi-factor authentication, fraud detection, and compliance protocols need to feel seamless, not paranoid.
Multi-channel is a must, not a feature

Your customers use the mobile app, the web platform, the branch, and sometimes phone banking. Inconsistency across channels frustrates users and increases support costs. True digital banking means unified experience everywhere.
Scale brings complexity

Retail banks serve millions of customers, each with different needs. Segmenting experience for different customer types, lifecycle stages, and risk profiles—without making the product feel fragmented—is a complex design problem.

Insurance UX is harder than it looks. The sector faces structural challenges that other financial services don't.
Products are inherently complex

A health insurance policy has premiums, deductibles, coinsurance, out-of-pocket maximums, network restrictions, and pre-authorisation requirements. Customers engage infrequently

Most people buy insurance once a year and hope they never need it. When they do need it—during a claim—they're stressed and just want help. Your UX needs to serve casual annual buyers and distressed claim filers equally well.
Claims are notoriously painful

The claims journey is often where insurers lose customer trust. Forms to fill, documents to collect, denials to explain. Poor claims UX doesn't just frustrate customers; it creates support costs and damages reputation.
Regulation and compliance are heavy
Insurance is heavily regulated. Disclosure requirements, fair pricing requirements, and consumer protection laws shape every interaction. Your UX has to satisfy regulators *and* customers.
Multi-stakeholder experience
Insurance isn't just B2C. Brokers, agents, and corporate clients all use your platform differently. Good insurance UX serves multiple audiences without fracturing the experience.

Building AI Products That Users Actually Trust and Use.
The AI Product Design Challenge: It's Not Just Engineering

AI is reshaping product development. But building a product around AI introduces challenges that traditional product design doesn't face: explainability, trust, error handling, and training users who don't understand how the system works.

The problem: Most AI startups are engineering-first. Founders and engineers are brilliant at building models and optimising algorithms. But they often ship products that users find confusing, unreliable, or hard to trust.

Users don't care how clever the model is. They care: Does this actually solve my problem? Can I understand what it's doing? What happens when it gets it wrong? Will it make my life easier or more complicated?
Design-led AI development starts with these questions. It puts user needs first and designs the product around trust, clarity, and actual utility.
What Design-Led AI Development Looks Like
Design-led AI development follows a specific rhythm:
1. User problem first, AI second.

Start with a real user problem. Then ask: does AI solve it better than a traditional approach? Some problems AI is perfect for. Others, it creates more friction than it solves. Good design answers this question early.
2. Design the UX before building the model.

How will users interact with the AI? What inputs do they provide? What outputs do they see? How do they know if the AI is working? These design questions should shape the model architecture, not the other way around.
3. Build trust through transparency.

Users need to understand what the AI is doing and why. Explainability doesn't mean showing the model weights. It means: showing confidence levels, explaining key factors in the decision, highlighting uncertainties, and making it easy for users to correct the AI if needed.
4. Design error handling and fallbacks.
AI will get things wrong. How does the user know? What can they do about it? Does it fail gracefully or catastrophically? Good design anticipates failure modes and designs graceful degradation.
5. Test with real users iteratively.
Prototypes, MVPs, and betas are tested with actual users. Does the AI solve their problem? Do they understand how to use it? Do they trust it? Iterate based on feedback.
Common AI Startup UX Mistakes
We see these patterns repeatedly:
The black box problem.
The AI makes a prediction but doesn't explain it. Users don't know if they can trust the output. This kills adoption.
Poor onboarding.
Users don't understand how to use the AI or what it can do. They get a confused first experience and ghost.
Unrealistic expectations.
Marketing oversells what the AI can do. Users get disappointed when reality falls short.
No error handling.
The AI makes a mistake but the interface doesn't make it obvious. Users end up making decisions based on bad data.
Over-automating the wrong thing.
Sometimes the best UX is to ask the user for input, not to automate everything. Good design finds the right balance.
Ignoring bias and fairness.
AI systems inherit biases from training data. If you don't design with fairness in mind, your product will discriminate. That's a PR disaster and a legal risk.

4. Culture & Leadership
Do leaders value design? Is user research embraced or seen as a cost? Are teams empowered to iterate, or do stakeholders micromanage every pixel?

Designers work in a silo; engineers build what they think is right; product owns the roadmap. Overcome it: Establish cross-functional rituals. Run joint workshops. Build shared understanding of user needs and constraints.

Every project starts from scratch; consistency is accidental. Overcome it: Start small - identify patterns in your current work. Build a lightweight design system. Iterate. Don't over-engineer.

sections.heading: The Design Maturity Model: Where Is Your Organisation on the Curve?
body: What Is Design Maturity and Why It Matters

Design maturity describes how systematically and strategically an organisation integrates design into its decision-making, product development, and operations. Organisations with low design maturity treat design as decoration or an afterthought—a function called in after strategy and engineering have moved on. Mature organisations embed design from day one, using user research and design thinking to inform every critical decision.

The maturity gap matters because it directly affects business outcomes: speed of delivery, product quality, user adoption, competitive differentiation, and ultimately, revenue. Organisations that invest in design capability ship faster, face fewer costly reworks, attract and retain better talent, and command premium pricing.
The Design Maturity Model is a diagnostic tool. It helps you see where your organisation sits on the curve and what the next level looks like.

sections.heading: The Five Levels of Design Maturity
body: Level 1: Ad Hoc

Design is reactive, project-by-project, with no consistency or process. Designers are brought in late, decisions are made without user research, and there is no design strategy. Each project looks different. Stakeholder opinions drive decisions, not user data. Design is seen as a cost centre, not a value driver.
Symptoms: Long rework cycles, poor user adoption, high support costs, no brand consistency.
Level 2: Defined

The organisation recognises design's value and begins to establish basic processes. There is a design function, some standards, and design is involved earlier in projects. User research happens occasionally. Design decisions are documented, but strategy is still informal. Leadership sees design as useful but not essential.
Symptoms: Better consistency, shorter feedback loops, but still some siloed working and limited strategic influence.
Level 3: Managed

Design is systematised. There is a clear design strategy aligned to business goals. User research is standard practice. A design system exists and is maintained. Designers sit with product and engineering teams, not in a separate silo. Design is measured—metrics track usability, adoption, and business impact. Governance exists to protect quality.
Symptoms: Faster delivery, higher adoption rates, consistent user experience, measurable design ROI.
Level 4: Integrated

Design is fully embedded in strategy, product, and operations. Design thinking shapes how the organisation solves problems, from customer experience to internal process improvement. Cross-functional teams are design-led. The design system is a competitive asset. Design metrics are board-level KPIs. Design talent is strategic hire.
Symptoms: Faster innovation, premium positioning, design-driven culture, high employee engagement.
Level 5: Design-Led

The organisation is design-first. Design and strategy are inseparable. Innovation is driven by deep user insight, prototyping, and iteration. Customers choose the brand because of its design and experience. Design capability attracts investment and partnerships. Failure is expected and learned from. The organisation competes on experience, not features.
Symptoms: Industry leadership, premium margins, strong brand equity, continuous innovation.
Signs Your Organisation Has a Design Maturity Problem
You may have a design maturity gap if:
•	Product launches are delayed by design rework cycles.
•	Users complain about difficulty using your products.
•	Each team has its own design standards—no consistency.
•	Design decisions are made in meetings, not based on user research.
•	Your design team reports to marketing, not product.
•	You ship features faster than users can learn them.
•	Design role is filled by whoever is available, not a dedicated professional.
•	Design strategy is something that happens after the product strategy is locked.
•	Competitors' products feel more polished and intuitive.
Why Organisations Stall at Certain Levels
Most organisations plateau at Level 2 or 3. Why?
Lack of executive sponsorship: Design maturity needs budget, headcount, and strategic attention. Without C-level backing, design remains a cost centre.
Siloed structure: Design sits separately from product and engineering. Collaboration is reactive, not embedded.
No design system or process: Without standards and tools, each project reinvents the wheel. Consistency and speed suffer.
Absence of design metrics: If you don't measure design impact, leadership sees it as subjective and expendable.
Hiring wrong skills: Organisations sometimes hire designers who can execute visuals but lack strategic thinking or research capability.
Culture misalignment: Some organisations say they value user-centred design but reward heroic delivery and technical complexity. The culture defeats the strategy.
How to Move Up the Maturity Curve
Moving up requires three things: leadership commitment, talent investment, and process discipline.
Start with a clear diagnosis.

Where does your organisation actually sit? Talk to designers, product managers, and engineering. Run a design audit. Look at user research spend, design system maturity, and cross-functional collaboration. Honest assessment is the first step.
Build a design strategy aligned to business goals.

Design maturity isn't about having prettier products. It's about solving user problems faster and better than competitors. Your design strategy should address: Who are the users we prioritise? What are their unmet needs? How will better design create competitive advantage? What metrics matter?
Invest in talent and process.

You need people with research, strategy, and systems thinking skills—not just visual designers. Invest in a design system. Establish rituals: user research, design critiques, usability testing, metrics reviews. Measure the impact of design on business outcomes.
Embed design early and deeply.

Design should inform strategy, not execute it after the fact. Designers should sit in product planning meetings, not get pulled in for a visual polish pass. Design critique should happen before engineering commits to direction.
Create a design-first culture.

Culture change is slower than process change, but it's the biggest unlock. Celebrate user-centred decisions. Reward learning from user feedback, not just speed. Share design impact stories. Make design everyone's responsibility, not a specialised function.

We've helped fintech, banking, insurance, and healthcare organisations move from ad hoc design to managed, integrated design operations. We build design systems, train teams, establish research practices, and embed design thinking into product development.
The result: faster delivery, higher adoption, better user satisfaction, and measurable business impact.

Why Digital Transformation Needs UX at Its Core

Most digital transformations fail. Industry analysts put the failure rate at 50–70%. The usual suspects: poor change management, misaligned stakeholders, technical debt, unrealistic timelines. But there's a quieter killer: UX is treated as a cosmetic layer, added after the technical architecture is baked in.

Here's the hard truth: If your transformation programme doesn't have UX built in from day one, you're building something users won't want to use. And if users won't use it, the transformation doesn't happen.

UX is not about making things pretty. It's about ensuring that the new system your organisation is moving to actually serves user needs better than the old one. Without that, you'll see resistance, workarounds, and poor adoption—all of which kill ROI.
How Poor UX Sinks Transformation Programmes

Consider a typical enterprise transformation: migrating from a legacy system to a cloud-based platform. Engineering and procurement own the timeline. IT architects design the technical architecture. The business sets the budget and timelines. Then, six weeks before go-live, UX gets called in.

What happens? The new system looks modern, but users find it harder to do their jobs. Navigation is unclear. Key workflows take more clicks. Critical data is buried. Users have to learn entirely new ways of doing things, but no one has invested in change management or training.

Result: Go-live becomes a crisis. Support costs spike. Users create workarounds, defeating the point of the modernisation. The business declares the transformation a partial success, when in fact it's costing more than it saves.
We've seen this story in fintech, banking, insurance, and government. The symptoms are always the same:
•	Low adoption rates in the weeks after go-live.
•	High support ticket volume—users can't figure out how to do basic tasks.
•	Users reverting to the old system or creating manual workarounds.
•	Staff resistance and frustration.
•	Delayed business process improvements because the underlying experience is broken.
What UX Delivers for Transformation Programmes
When UX is embedded from the start, it changes the trajectory of a transformation.
User research and insight.

Before you build anything, you need to understand what users actually do today and what they need from the new system. Research uncovers critical workflows, pain points, and adoption risks early—when they're cheap to fix.
Journey design and architecture.

Journey mapping helps you see the end-to-end experience from a user's perspective. You spot where the new system requires users to change behaviour, and you design the experience to make that transition as smooth as possible. You identify critical moments that could derail adoption.
Change readiness and adoption strategy.

UX teams work with organisational change management to prepare users. Training materials, onboarding experiences, and support touchpoints are designed around how users will actually interact with the new system. This dramatically improves adoption velocity.
Stakeholder alignment.

User research and design artefacts (wireframes, prototypes, journey maps) create a shared language across technical teams, business stakeholders, and end users. Everyone sees the same vision of what success looks like. This reduces scope creep and late-stage surprises.
De-risking the programme.

Usability testing and feedback loops happen before go-live, not after. You find problems when there's still time to fix them. You build confidence among users before they have to live with the new system in production.
How to Embed UX Into a Transformation Programme
If you're planning a transformation, here's what good looks like:
1. Bring UX in at the discovery phase.

Before architects design the technical system, UX should be conducting user research, mapping current journeys, and identifying user needs. This informs the requirements the technical teams will build against.
2. Make UX a core part of governance.

UX should be represented in steering committees and architecture reviews. Design decisions should be reviewed alongside technical ones. If the roadmap includes a feature that creates UX debt, it should be visible and debated.
3. Create cross-functional product teams.
Don't hand designs to engineers for implementation. Work in integrated teams where UX, engineering, and product collaborate continuously. Design and engineering decisions should inform each other.
4. Build a design system and component library.
A shared design system ensures consistency, speeds up delivery, and reduces downstream rework. Components built once, reused everywhere.
5. Test with real users early and often.
Don't wait until beta testing. Run usability tests on prototypes, designs, and the working product. Iterate based on feedback. Users are your best quality assurance.
6. Invest in change management and training.
Work with your change management team to design training, onboarding, and support. Make sure users understand not just how to use the system, but why it matters and how it makes their jobs better.
Common Transformation Mistakes
Watch out for these pitfalls:
UX as an afterthought.
If UX comes in during the design phase, you're already late. The technical architecture is set, requirements are locked. You can't change the hard stuff anymore.
No user research budget.
Some programmes try to save money by skipping research. This always backfires. You end up building the wrong thing or building the right thing wrong.
Skipping user testing.
Testing before go-live is an insurance policy. Skip it and you're gambling with adoption.
Disconnected UX team.
If UX sits separately from product and engineering, you'll see siloed work and late integration. Integration happens best when teams sit together.
Over-automating for the wrong user.
Sometimes automation serves the business (cost reduction) but harms users. Good UX finds the balance.

As embedded UX partners, we lead research, design strategy, and user experience design. We sit on the transformation steering committee and ensure user needs are front and centre.
As UX coaches, we work with your internal teams to build UX capability—training designers and product managers in research, design thinking, and collaboration practices.
Either way, the goal is the same: to ensure your transformation is designed around what users actually need, not just what the technical architecture makes easy.

Nonprofit organizations often lack the resources and expertise to build great digital experiences. But your digital presence directly impacts donations, volunteer engagement, and your mission's reach. Why Nonprofits Need Digital Strategy

The nonprofit landscape has shifted. Donors expect seamless online experiences. Volunteers find opportunities digitally. Impact is communicated through content. Fundraising happens through digital channels. Yet many nonprofits operate with outdated websites, fragmented tools, and no coherent digital strategy.
The result: lost donations, missed volunteer engagement, and impact that's harder to communicate. A strategic, well-designed digital presence is no longer optional - it's essential.

sections.heading: Common Nonprofit Digital Mistakes
body: Mistake 1: Website as an afterthought

Many nonprofits build a website to have one, but it doesn't serve donors, volunteers, or stakeholders. Information is buried. Donation flows are unclear. Mobile experience is broken. The website becomes a cost center, not a tool.
Mistake 2: Treating donors like any visitor

Major donors have different needs than first-time visitors. Repeat donors need to understand impact. Corporate partners need data. Yet most nonprofit websites treat everyone the same. Digital strategy means understanding different audience segments and designing for them.
Mistake 3: Poor donation experience

A complex, multi-step donation flow kills conversions. Many nonprofits use generic payment platforms with no nonprofit context. Donors abandon if the experience feels clunky or untrusted. UX matters here.
Mistake 4: No content strategy
Nonprofits often have great stories but no plan to tell them. Content is sporadic, inconsistent, or absent. Impact isn't communicated. Digital channels aren't leveraged for awareness or engagement.
Mistake 5: Tools without strategy

Nonprofits adopt CRMs, email platforms, donation systems, and social tools - but they operate in silos. There's no unified view of supporters. Data isn't connected. The tech stack becomes fragmented and expensive.
The Role of UX in Nonprofit Fundraising and Engagement

Good UX isn't a luxury for nonprofits - it's a revenue multiplier. A one-second faster donation page increases conversion by 1-2%. Clear impact communication drives repeat donations. A strong volunteer onboarding experience reduces drop-off. Intuitive supporter engagement tools increase lifetime value.
Donation Experience

We design donation flows that convert. This means: minimal steps, clear trust signals (security, impact data), options for recurring donations, and post-donation engagement. We have seen nonprofits increase donation conversion by 15-30% through UX improvements alone.
Supporter Engagement
From volunteer sign-up to event registration to monthly supporter updates - we design experiences that keep supporters engaged. Engagement drives retention and lifetime value.
Impact Communication

The most powerful nonprofit tool is impact data. We help you design ways to communicate impact - dashboards, impact reports, case studies, before/after narratives. This builds trust and drives repeat support.
Building a Content Strategy That Communicates Impact
Content is how nonprofits tell their story. But without strategy, it's just noise.
Define Your Narrative
What's your core story? Who benefits? What change are you creating? A strong nonprofit narrative connects supporters to mission. We help you define and articulate that narrative across channels.
Know Your Audiences
Donors, volunteers, beneficiaries, corporate partners, government funders - each has different needs. Content strategy means understanding what each audience needs to hear and where they look.
Create Impact Content

Stories of beneficiaries changed. Data on outcomes. Footage of work in action. Long-form content (impact reports, research) builds authority. Short-form content (social, email) drives engagement. We help you plan content that works across channels.
Amplify Through Digital Channels

Website, email, social media, YouTube - each channel serves a purpose. Content strategy means knowing what goes where, when, and why. It means repurposing content across channels and measuring what works.

sections.heading: Heineken: B2B E-Commerce UX/UI Design
body: The Challenge

Heineken needed to modernise the way wholesale customers—bars, restaurants, hotels, and bottle shops—placed orders. They had invested in an SAP e-commerce platform as the backend, but the frontend user interface was generic and didn't meet the needs of wholesale buyers.

The problem: Wholesale ordering is different from retail e-commerce. Wholesale customers buy in volume, have negotiated pricing, manage multiple locations, and need flexible ordering patterns. A standard e-commerce UI wasn't going to work.

Heineken engaged Sand Dollar Design to create a custom, headless UI that reimagined the B2B ordering experience—making it fast, intuitive, and tailored to how wholesale customers actually do business.
Our Approach
We took a discovery-first, user-led approach to B2B e-commerce design:
1. User Research with Wholesale Customers

We interviewed and shadowed 10+ wholesale buyers across different customer segments (on-premise, off-premise, independent, chains). We learned their buying patterns, pain points, and what would make ordering easier.
2. Competitive and Comparative Analysis
We studied how other B2B platforms (e-commerce, supply chain, distribution) served wholesale customers, identifying best practices and opportunities for differentiation.
3. Journey Mapping and Requirements
We mapped end-to-end buying journeys and translated user needs into product requirements: account management, order history, volume pricing, delivery tracking, etc.
4. Wireframing and Design
We designed the complete user interface—from product discovery and browsing, to cart, checkout, account management, and order tracking. We designed for both desktop and mobile.
5. User Testing and Refinement
Designs were tested with wholesale customers. We refined interaction patterns, information architecture, and key flows based on feedback.
6. Headless Integration with SAP Backend
We ensured the UI cleanly integrated with the SAP backend via APIs, allowing the design to be implemented independently of backend changes.
What We Did
•	Conducted user research interviews with 10+ wholesale customers across 4 segments.
•	Mapped 5 critical wholesale buying journeys.
•	Created comparative analysis of B2B e-commerce platforms.
•	Designed 40+ screens (desktop and mobile) covering the full buying experience.
•	Built an interactive prototype for testing and feedback.
•	Conducted 2 rounds of user testing (n=5 per round).
•	Created API specifications to guide SAP integration.
•	Delivered comprehensive UI design system and component library.
Key Outcomes
Post-launch, the B2B platform delivered measurable improvements:
•	Improved order placement—wholesale customers completed orders in significantly fewer steps.
•	Better product discovery—customers found products they wanted to buy more easily.
•	Increased order frequency—the easier experience encouraged more frequent ordering.
•	Higher customer satisfaction—wholesale customers rated the platform highly.
•	Reduced support burden—fewer customer service calls about how to place orders.
Deliverables
•	User research report and wholesale buying journey maps.
•	Competitive and comparative analysis.
•	Information architecture and wireframes.
•	High-fidelity UI designs for desktop and mobile.
•	Interactive prototype for testing and validation.
•	User testing findings and recommendations.
•	API specifications for headless integration.
•	UI design system and Figma component library.

sections.heading: Mukuru: Mobile App Rebrand and Redesign
body: The Challenge

Mukuru, a leading fintech and mobile money platform across Africa, underwent a major brand refresh. The new brand identity needed to be reflected across all customer touchpoints—including their mobile application, used daily by tens of thousands of customers for money transfers, bill payments, and account management.

The complexity: A mobile money app isn't just a visual redesign. The app sits in a highly regulated environment, handles sensitive financial transactions, and serves a diverse user base across multiple countries with varying digital literacy. Rebrand requirements had to align with usability, compliance, and the real constraints of how users actually interact with money management apps.
Sand Dollar Design was brought in to lead the UX and UI redesign, ensuring the new brand identity enhanced rather than compromised the user experience.
Our Approach
We took a strategic, user-centred approach:
1. UX Research with Real Users

We conducted in-depth user interviews and usability sessions with active Mukuru customers across target markets. We observed how they used the app, what journeys were critical, and where they experienced friction. This research informed every design decision.
2. Information Architecture & Journey Mapping

We mapped the user journeys through core workflows: money transfers, bill payments, account management, and transaction history. We identified opportunities to simplify navigation and improve flow clarity.
3. Design System & Visual Consistency
We built a comprehensive design system that married the new brand identity with mobile-first, user-friendly design principles. Components were designed for consistency and scalability across the app.
4. UI Redesign
We redesigned the interface to reflect the new brand while improving usability. Typography, colour, icons, and layout were refined based on user feedback and accessibility standards.
5. User Testing & Iteration
Designs were tested with real users before handoff to engineering. We refined interaction patterns, call-to-action placement, and critical flows based on feedback.
What We Did
•	Conducted user research interviews with 12+ Mukuru customers across 3 markets.
•	Mapped 8 critical user journeys through the app.
•	Built a design system with 60+ components (buttons, inputs, cards, modals, etc.).
•	Redesigned 25+ screens across the full app.
•	Created high-fidelity prototypes of key flows.
•	Conducted 2 rounds of user testing (n=6 per round).
•	Delivered comprehensive UI design specs and Figma component library.
Key Outcomes
Post-launch, Mukuru saw marked improvements in user experience:
•	Improved clarity on critical journeys—users completed money transfer flows with fewer steps and less confusion.
•	Brand alignment—the app now visually represents Mukuru's refreshed brand identity while maintaining usability.
•	Better accessibility—updated contrast ratios and typography improved readability.
•	Faster time-to-transaction—streamlined flows reduced friction in high-frequency user actions.
•	Positive user feedback—app ratings improved post-redesign.
Deliverables
•	User research report and journey maps.
•	Design system documentation and Figma component library.
•	High-fidelity UI designs for all app screens.
•	Interactive prototypes for key user flows.
•	User testing findings and recommendations.
•	Implementation specs and design handoff documentation.

•	Poor navigation and information architecture.
•	Outdated, cluttered visual interface.
•	Confusing workflows for accessing reports and analytics.
•	High support burden—users needed hand-holding to accomplish tasks.
The bank needed to modernise the platform without disrupting daily operations or requiring a full rebuild. Sand Dollar Design was engaged to improve the UX and UI of the existing system.
Our Approach
We took a pragmatic, user-centred approach to legacy system modernisation:
1. Research with Internal Users
We conducted interviews and shadowing sessions with 8 internal users across different departments (finance, risk, operations). We observed actual workflows and identified pain points.
2. Heuristic Evaluation
We reviewed the existing system against usability principles and identified specific UX problems: navigation structure, label clarity, visual hierarchy, and workflow efficiency.
3. Information Architecture Redesign
We restructured navigation and information grouping to match how users actually think about the data, not the technical database structure.
4. Visual Modernisation
We updated the UI to a modern, clean aesthetic while maintaining compatibility with the underlying WebFocus platform.
5. User Testing & Refinement
